papers.title: Proximal Femur Cut-Out Treatment, Re-Fixation or Arthroplasty: Which Yields Better Outcomes? Insights from 143 Patients from the PIPPAS Study
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Arthroplasty is the standard of care for proximal femur cut-out injuries (FCO). Re-fixation with an intramedullary nail has been proposed as a joint-preserving, less-invasive alternative. However, it remains unclear which strategy, re-fixation or arthroplasty, leads to better outcomes regarding one-year mortality, surgical and medical complications, and functional recovery. Methods: This multicentre prospective observational cohort (PIPPAS sub-analysis) enrolled 165 patients with FCO from January 2021 to December 2023. After excluding nonoperative management and isolated hardware removal, 143 surgically treated patients were analysed: re-fixation with revision intramedullary nailing (n = 22) versus conversion arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty/total hip arthroplasty) (n = 121). Results: Patients were elderly (median age 86 years), predominantly female (82.5%), and frail (80.9% ASA III–IV). Baseline characteristics and cut-out morphology were similar between groups. A nail was the implant involved in all FCO. One-year mortality was numerically lower after re-fixation than after arthroplasty (1/22 [4.5%] versus 28/121 [23.1%]; unadjusted p = 0.047), but this comparison was based on only one death in the re-fixation group and was not statistically significant after multivariable adjustment (arthroplasty versus re-fixation: OR 7.93, 95% CI 0.80–78.20; p = 0.076). Fixation failure was more frequent after re-fixation (3/22 [13.6%] versus 3/121 [2.5%]; p = 0.047)., and hospital stay was shorter (median 8.3 versus 14.2 days; p < 0.001). Overall surgical (22.7% versus 33.1%; p = 0.456) and medical (54.5% versus 72.7%; p = 0.087) complication rates did not differ significantly, although infection (13.2%) and dislocation (9.9%) were clinically relevant in the arthroplasty group. Weight-bearing restrictions were more frequent after re-fixation, but there were no significant between-group differences in mobility decline, change in residence, or EQ-5D at one year. Univariate analysis associated male sex (OR 2.76, p = 0.036), higher ASA (OR 2.934, p = 0.010), and age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (OR 1.340, p = 0.006) with increased mortality, while higher admission hemoglobin was protective. In the multivariable mortality model, male sex, higher ASA grade, higher age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index, and lower admission hemoglobin were associated with increased mortality. Arthroplasty was associated with a non-significant increase in the odds of mortality compared with re-fixation (OR 7.93, 95% CI 0.80–78.20; p = 0.076); this estimate should not be interpreted as evidence of no association or as a treatment effect. Conclusions: Re-fixation with an intramedullary nail augmented with bone graft offers a viable joint-preserving alternative to arthroplasty in selected patients with FCO. Re-fixation was associated with shorter hospital stay and numerically lower, but statistically fragile, one-year mortality; however, fixation failure was more frequent after re-fixation. These data do not establish superiority of either treatment. Careful patient selection, assessment of residual bone stock and acetabular damage, and surgical technique to optimize bone purchase are critical.

papers.title: Midterm Outcomes of Jumbo Acetabular Cups Without Structural Bone Grafting in Selected Hartofilakidis Type A and B1 Dysplastic Hips
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Jumbo acetabular cups are widely used in revision total hip arthroplasty (THA), but evidence on their use in primary THA for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is limited. This study aimed to report the midterm clinical, radiographic and survival outcomes of graft-free reconstruction with jumbo cups in selected patients with Hartofilakidis Type A and B1 DDH. Methods: Sixty-four patients (68 hips) with Hartofilakidis Type A or B1 DDH-related osteoarthritis underwent primary THA with jumbo cups (≥64 mm in men, ≥60 mm in women) between January 2018 and November 2021, after adequate anterior and posterior column support had been confirmed intraoperatively. Functional outcomes (mHHS, HOOS, SF-36), hip center position, host bone coverage and implant survival were evaluated. The hip center and leg length discrepancy (LLD) were compared with the normal contralateral hip in 50 patients with unilateral THA. Results: The mean follow-up was 5.0 ± 1.0 years. In the 66 hips retaining the original component, the mHHS improved from 52.1 ± 13.8 to 89.8 ± 6.2 (mean change, 37.7; 95% CI, 34.0–41.5), and all HOOS and SF-36 domains improved significantly (p < 0.001). The vertical and horizontal centers of rotation decreased from 31.5 ± 4.8 to 24.1 ± 4.6 mm and from 44.3 ± 4.4 to 33.8 ± 4.2 mm, respectively; the mean host bone coverage was 85.7 ± 6.7%. Compared with the normal contralateral hip, the operated hip center was 9.5 mm (95% CI, 8.6–10.3) superior and 2.6 mm (2.2–2.9) medial, and LLD decreased from −21.9 ± 6.9 to −5.3 ± 4.6 mm. Complications occurred in 5 of 68 hips (7.4%), including two acetabular revisions. The 5-year survival was 96.5% (95% CI, 86.4–99.1) for revision for any reason and 97.9% (86.1–99.7) for revision for aseptic loosening. Conclusions: In selected patients with Hartofilakidis Type A or B1 dysplasia and adequate anterior and posterior column support, graft-free reconstruction with jumbo acetabular cups was associated with an improved hip center position, good midterm function and high implant survival. Comparative studies are needed to determine its value relative to bone grafting and high hip center techniques.

papers.title: Sustainable Aviation Fuels for Gas Turbine Decarbonization: A Critical Review of Thermodynamic Performance, Fleet Emissions, and Engine Integration
papers.abstract: The aviation sector contributes approximately 2%–3% of global anthropogenic CO 2 emissions, with projected growth potentially tripling emissions by 2050 in the absence of mitigation strategies. Sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs) represent the most viable near‐term pathway for decarbonizing gas turbine–based aviation. This review provides a comprehensive and critical assessment of major SAF pathways, including Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA), Fischer–Tropsch (FT) fuels, and alcohol‐to‐jet fuels, in comparison with conventional JET‐A. A key contribution of this work is the integration of thermochemical fuel analysis with a global fleet emission dataset comprising over 150 aircraft–airline combinations across more than 10 countries. Thermodynamic cycle simulations for a representative turbojet engine indicate that FT fuels can reduce CO 2 mass fraction by 8.3% and NOx emissions by up to 26% relative to JET‐A, while maintaining near‐identical thermal performance. Fleet‐level analysis further reveals that modern high‐bypass turbofan engines significantly reduce CO and hydrocarbon emissions but may exhibit up to 3.6 times higher NOx emissions compared to regional aircraft, highlighting a critical design trade‐off. Lifecycle analysis indicates that HEFA and FT fuels can achieve 60%–80% CO 2 reduction, although their deployment is constrained by feedstock availability and production costs, which are currently 4–6 times higher than conventional fuels. This review identifies key challenges in combustor design, emission trade‐offs, certification constraints, and economic scalability. Finally, the study highlights the role of digital twin frameworks and 100% SAF certification pathways as critical enablers for achieving net‐zero aviation targets by 2050.

papers.title: Effect of Process Co-Factors on Surface Roughness of Subscale Feature Surfaces in Laser PBF of Ti6Al4V
papers.abstract: The as-built vertical surface of laser powder bed fused (PBF-LB/M) Ti6Al4V governs several critical properties like fatigue performance, fluid friction, osseointegration, etc., yet how surfaces of subscale features, such as thin walls and gaps, respond to process cofactors, isolated from confounding effects, remains poorly quantified. This study extracted 323 line-based (Ra, Rz) and areal (Sa, Sz, Spc, Str) roughness measurements from 143 Ti6Al4V ELI thin-wall and thin-gap PBF-LB/M coupons spanning three feature sizes, two layer thicknesses, two build alignments, and nine build-plate zones, using a structured white-light profilometer; cofactor effects were dissociated with ANOVA, Welch t-tests, and Gaussian mixture modeling, and corroborated with optical microstructure and Vickers microhardness. Vertical line scans gave 14% higher multi-line Ra than horizontal line scans (mean areal Sa 5.91 μm); the narrowest 200 μm gap was significantly rougher than wider gaps; changing from the 30 μm to the 60 μm layer-thickness parameter set raised thin-wall roughness 15–19%; gas-flow-aligned walls were up to 23% rougher than recoater-aligned walls; and the texture aspect ratio was bimodal in thin walls, with about 21% strongly anisotropic, but not in thin gaps. Comparison with the companion dimensional data showed that process variables affected roughness and dimensional deviation differently: 60 μm layers produced rougher yet thinner walls, and the base improved gap-width consistency without significantly changing gap roughness. Optical microscopy and microhardness of sectioned thin walls showed that the density of partially sintered particles, the width of a lighter-etching edge microstructural zone, and the near-edge hardness deficit all decreased as wall thickness increased. These trends are consistent with a wall-thickness-dependent heat-conduction pathway, which was inferred rather than measured, and offer a potential mechanistic basis for subscale feature design.
